contributions.statement: When tracking how coding-agent adoption affects Java code health, report raw architectural smell counts, unstable-dependency counts and LOC separately, because smell density fell 6.7% after adoption only because code grew about 13% while smell counts did not change detectably.
contributions.evidence: §4.2 Table 1 (Borusyak ATT -6.98%, p=0.004) and §4.5 Fig. 4 (raw counts +1.1%, p=0.82; LOC +12.8%, p=0.003; packages +9.7%); 151 Java repos, staggered DiD with matched controls. Audit: observational, Lee bound includes zero.

contributions.statement: In mature Java repositories, the first measurable effect of agent adoption is code-volume growth rather than architectural decay, so watch LOC and unstable-dependency counts (raw +5.8%, not significant after Holm) beyond six months.
contributions.evidence: §4.3, §4.5: smell-count CI roughly -8% to +11% with no equivalence test (audit), so 'no increase' is not demonstrated; UD rise labelled suggestive.

reason: The only causal Java study in the batch; its main contribution is a measurement warning that density metrics hide code growth, which applies directly to Sonar-style dashboards.
